opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I don't think there was a single moment where a switch flipped. It was more a gradual feeling that the questions I cared about most were starting to outgrow the shape of what a university lab can do on its own.

I love academia. Being at NYU gave me freedom: I could chase ideas that weren't fashionable yet, work with students who challenge you every day, and think on a longer time horizon than a product roadmap allows. A lot of what I believe about representation learning, about vision, about how models should understand the world, came from that environment. So it was never "academia is bad, I need to leave."

But over the past few years the nature of the research changed. If you believe, as I do, that the next big step isn't just scaling language models but building systems that actually understand the physical, visual world, then you need very large-scale experiments to test that belief. You need compute, you need engineering infrastructure, and you need a team that can iterate fast and stay focused on one ambitious bet for years. In a university you can write the first paper that points in a direction. It's much harder to carry that direction all the way to something that really works at scale.

So the judgment I made was less about the platform and more about the question: am I still able to answer the question I care about where I am? When I started feeling the honest answer was "only partially," I knew I had to consider something different.

There was also a personal element. When you're young as a researcher, you optimize for papers and recognition. At some point you start asking what you actually want to leave behind. For me it's less about another paper and more about whether this idea becomes real. That pushed me to accept more risk.

And I don't see it as fully leaving. The academic mindset of being curious, open, willing to be wrong, and caring about students and the community is something I want to bring with me. Ideally the line between the two worlds becomes blurrier, not sharper.

r001.rationale: The response says NYU gave him freedom to pursue ideas, but does not clearly say the university gave him room to discover what he wanted to pursue.

r002.rationale: The response describes limits on scaling research at a university, but does not identify the risk of a “middle-paper trap” from further exploring his existing direction as the signal to move on.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I never framed it as "leaving" the university. I still think of myself as a professor first. For me the question was more like: what does this particular piece of work need right now, and does the university environment actually provide it?

When I came back to academia from FAIR, I made that choice deliberately. I wanted the freedom to work on problems where the payoff is uncertain, to train students, to think in longer timescales. And a lot of what I care about—understanding why certain architectures work, representation learning, the fundamentals—really does fit a university. You don't need ten thousand GPUs to have a good idea.

But over the last couple of years, something shifted. The gap between what you can do with a few hundred GPUs and what the frontier labs can do started to matter for the questions themselves. Some questions only reveal themselves at scale. If you want to know whether a method still works when you go up two orders of magnitude, you can't answer that with a workshop paper and a hunch. At some point I had to be honest with myself: there were experiments I kept writing on the whiteboard that I knew we'd never actually run.

The second signal was about people. I was watching my students and collaborators, and the most interesting conversations were happening across the boundary—between academia and the labs, not inside either one. So the question became less "university or not" and more "how do I be in a position where the ideas can actually get tested, and where the people I want to work with are?"

And the third thing, frankly, was timing. There are windows in a field where the important decisions about what gets built are being made, and if you're not close to where that's happening, you end up studying the artifacts afterward rather than shaping them. I felt that window was open now, and it might not be open in the same way in five years.

So it wasn't one moment. It was accumulating evidence that the problems I cared most about had outgrown the resources I had, and that I could keep the parts of the academic life I valued—the curiosity, the mentorship, the willingness to be wrong in public—while borrowing the scale from somewhere else. I'd rather do that than slowly become someone who only works on problems that fit the budget.

r002.rationale: The response cites experiments that could not be run at university scale and the risk of limiting work to budget-fitting problems. It does not identify further exploration of his existing direction or a “middle-paper trap” as a signal to move beyond the university.

astra-6.text:
For me, the question was less whether I should leave the university and more what kind of environment the next stage of my research needed. A university gives you a lot of freedom to explore ideas, and that’s incredibly valuable. But you also have to ask: can I actually test those ideas at the scale where the important questions start to show up?

If your research increasingly depends on compute, data, and a team that can build things together, then the platform becomes part of the research problem. You might have a promising idea, but without the ability to run the right experiments, you can’t really learn whether it works.

So I wouldn’t say there’s one clear moment when you know. It’s more a gradual realization that the gap between what you want to investigate and what you can execute is getting larger. For me, that’s the signal to consider a different environment—somewhere that lets me keep asking open-ended questions while also being able to follow through on them.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, it was less about deciding that the university was no longer useful and more about asking what environment I needed for the next stage of my work. A university gives you room to explore, to develop your taste, and to learn how to ask questions independently. Those are things I value a lot.

But there’s a point where you want to take an idea further, and the constraints start to matter: the resources you can access, the people you can work with, and how quickly you can test something at scale. Then the question becomes, am I still choosing problems because they’re the most interesting ones, or because they fit the platform I’m on?

I wouldn’t say there was one clear moment. It was more a gradual recognition that a different environment might let me pursue the questions I cared about more directly. That doesn’t mean leaving the intellectual values of academia behind. You want to carry those with you.
